house-churches.title: Terrace House 2, Ephesus (frescoed room)
house-churches.location: Ephesus, western Turkey (ancient Roman Asia Minor)
house-churches.period: Core structure 1st century BCE/CE, continuously inhabited and remodeled through the 3rd century CE — overlapping this world's own c. 70-200 CE span
house-churches.story: An actual excavated Roman-era residential block built into the hillside opposite the Library of Celsus — a real, multi-room private house from the Greek East with its original painted wall decoration still visible, the same kind of domestic space a household leader like Chloe would have opened for a fellowship gathering. Some of the surviving fresco decoration visible in photos is later restoration-era work (2nd-3rd c.), not original to the earliest phase.
house-churches.author: José Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro
house-churches.attribution: Photo by José Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
house-churches.note: Replaced 2026-07-24: the first file pulled for this slot (same site, different photo) turned out to be a close-up of loose marble tile fragments, not a usable architectural view. Verified as genuinely mislabeled-for-purpose (not a download error) via Commons category metadata before swapping to this wider room view from the same verified category.

alexandria.title: Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa (tomb corridor)
alexandria.period: Carved 2nd century CE, used into the 4th century CE — squarely inside this world's c. 150-400 CE span
alexandria.story: Alexandria's own funerary architecture from exactly this era: a rock-cut tomb corridor with carved burial niches, the same complex whose main chamber literally fuses Egyptian funerary gods (Anubis, Apis) with Greek mythological forms inside a Roman-style architectural frame — a physical embodiment of the same intellectual synthesis the Catechetical School was working within.
alexandria.author: Roland Unger
alexandria.attribution: Photo by Roland Unger, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

syriac.title: Dura-Europos house-church (domus ecclesiae)
syriac.period: Converted from a private house into a church c. 232-256 CE — the earliest archaeologically identified Christian house-church/baptistery in the world
syriac.story: A real Roman-Syrian frontier garrison town sitting exactly in this world's own Mesopotamian frontier setting, giving Yausep's Syriac-speaking, Diatessaron-centered tradition a genuine physical home. (Checked and rejected: the visible citadel/walls at Şanlıurfa, ancient Edessa, are Abbasid/Mamluk/Ottoman-era rebuilds, not period fabric, despite being the correct location.)
syriac.author: Heretiq
syriac.attribution: Photo by Heretiq, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

empire.title: Hagia Irene (Church of the Holy Peace)
empire.period: Tradition holds it was founded under Constantine I in the 4th century; current fabric is largely Justinian's 6th-century rebuild after the Nika riots
empire.story: The oldest surviving church in Constantinople and the only Byzantine-era church in the city never converted into a mosque — the genuine physical church tied to Constantine's founding acts in the very city Marius travels to as Deacon of the Letters. (Checked and rejected: San Giovanni in Laterano's photographable facade today is Galilei's 1735 Baroque rebuild, nothing period-visible left.)
empire.author: Gryffindor
empire.attribution: Photo by Gryffindor, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (attribution not legally required, credited as good practice)

desert.title: Monastery of Saint Macarius the Great
desert.period: Founded late 4th century CE, on the same ground Papnoute's world represents — but honestly, no standing 4th-5th century fabric survives; the visible keep (qasr) dates 1069-1196 and the churches were rebuilt in the 7th, 11th, and 20th centuries
desert.story: The authentic historical site of Desert Monasticism, still an active monastery today — but a later-rebuilt structure on the original ground, not original fabric. (A more period-authentic alternative, the Kellia ruins, was found but its Commons license looks like an unverified scan from a book rather than the uploader's own photo, so it wasn't used here pending proper rights clearance.)
desert.author: Faris El-Gwely
desert.attribution: Photo by Faris El-Gwely, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bethlehem.title: Grotto of St. Jerome
bethlehem.location: Beneath the Church of St. Catherine, Bethlehem, physically adjoining the Grotto of the Nativity
bethlehem.period: The cave itself is the traditional site of Jerome's residence and Vulgate translation work, 382-420 CE; the altars and decoration visible today (including one dedicated to Paula and Eustochium) are later medieval/Franciscan additions
bethlehem.story: The actual cave where Jerome lived and worked on his translation, continuously identified with him since antiquity — and the visible altar dedicated to Paula and Eustochium is a striking direct match to this world's own household and its Representative, Albina.
bethlehem.author: Dennis G. Jarvis (archer10)
bethlehem.attribution: Photo by Dennis G. Jarvis, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
